# Lucas chain

- [Español](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encadenamiento_de_Lucas)
 [Edit links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q6696364#sitelinks-wikipedia)                          From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia   Restricted type of addition chain

In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), a **Lucas chain** is a restricted type of [addition chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addition_chain), named for the French mathematician [Édouard Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Lucas). It is a [sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence)

      a  0   ,  a  1   ,  a  2   ,  a  3   , …   {\displaystyle a_{0},a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},\ldots }

that satisfies *a*0=1, and, for each *k* > 0,

      a  k   =  a  i   +  a  j   ,   {\displaystyle a_{k}=a_{i}+a_{j},}

and either

      a  i   =  a  j     or   |  a  i   −  a  j   | =  a  m     {\displaystyle a_{i}=a_{j}{\text{ or }}\vert a_{i}-a_{j}\vert =a_{m}}

for some *i*, *j*, *m* < *k*.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_chain#cite_note-G169-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_chain#cite_note-2)

The sequence of powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...) and the [Fibonacci sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_sequence) (with a slight adjustment of the starting point 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ...) are simple examples of Lucas chains.

Lucas chains were introduced by [Peter Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Montgomery_(mathematician)) in 1983.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_chain#cite_note-3) They are analogous to [addition chains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addition_chain), in that just as an addition chain A that ends with n allows for evaluating an in len(*A*) steps, a Lucas chain C that ends with n allow for evaluating the [Lucas sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence) terms {*U*, *V* }*n* (*P*, *Q*) in len(*C*) steps.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_chain#cite_note-4)

Just like the addition chain, a basic method for computing a Lucas chain that ends with n is via the *binary method*, similar to [exponentiation by squaring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponentiation_by_squaring). This gives a chain length of *O*(log *n*). Shorter chains can be obtained using a range of other methods such as Montgomery's PRAC. Because the process of finding a better chain is expensive, good chains are usually precomputed.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_chain#cite_note-PZ06-5) DJ Bernstein mentions a number of Lucas chain-based schemes in 2017.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_chain#cite_note-6): §4.8.2

If *L*(*n*) is the length of the shortest Lucas chain for n, then Kutz has shown that most n do not have *L* < (1-ε) logφ(*n*), where φ is the [Golden ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_chain#cite_note-G169-1)
